16.0.s.en: (3) The parable of the prodigal son

16.0.0.en: Christ gave His disciples a parable about the importance of preparing for eternity by faithfulness in our earthly life, which is the parable of the unjust steward. He tells us of a rich man who appointed a steward to manage his affairs, but the steward was not faithful and exploited his master's money to satisfy his desires. So he wasted and squandered this money, and some told his master of his steward's unfaithfulness.

16.1.0.en: The master called his steward and confronted him with the charge of stealing his money, and demanded that he give an account of his stewardship because he would dismiss him from his work.

16.1.1.en: Prepare, my brother, for this moment when the demons accuse you, and God decides to end your life and demands that you give an account of all your past deeds, and even your words and thoughts. So take refuge in repentance every day and do everything you can to leave your sins, and you will receive forgiveness in the sacrament of confession; continue in the life of repentance and do not fear death.

16.2.0.en: "Dig": that is, to dig the ground with a hoe.

16.2.2.en: The unfaithful steward thought about the decision of dismissal that he faced and what he would do after that: he could not work as an ordinary laborer, digging the ground with a hoe and farming it, since after having been the manager of all these properties he would become a simple laborer; and on the other hand he could not get his needs by begging and asking alms.

16.2.3.en: This steward who robbed his master said that he could not work as a laborer because he was lazy, and could not beg because he was proud. All these are bad traits, but the only virtue he had was that he thought carefully to solve his problem, and he arrived at wrong human solutions, namely robbing his master so that those who shared in the embezzlement would honor him after he was dismissed. He is wicked and his devices are wicked, but his distinction was in not giving in and in seeking a solution.

16.3.0.en: His human thinking guided him to go further in robbing his master by giving up his rights to those who leased his land, that is, honoring these tenants at his master's expense. So he called one who was responsible for paying the master a hundred baths of oil each year (the bath is about 23 liters) and gave him the document or bill that established the master's right, for him to tear it up and write fifty instead; and so with another who was to give a hundred measures of wheat (the measure is about 230 liters), and he said to him, tear up the bill and write eighty; and so with the rest of the tenants. They rejoiced at this concession and promised to honor him after his dismissal from the stewardship.

16.4.0.en: "Children of this world": the children of the world who walk in evil.

16.4.1.en: "Children of light": the children of God, who is the true light, and who walk in the light of God's commandments.

16.4.2.en: The master admired the wisdom of this wicked steward and commended him, not for his evil and treachery but for his wisdom in getting himself out of the problem of dismissal. It is clear that the one who commended him is his master in the parable and not Christ, because Christ does not commend evil.

16.4.3.en: And Christ commented that the wicked children of the world, who use theft and treachery to achieve their goals, care for their future more than the children of light, that is, the children of God, in their preparing for eternity by doing good and righteousness. Learn from the conduct of those around you, and acquire their virtues, and be careful not to fall into the conduct of the wicked, lest their painful fate confront you.

16.5.0.en: "Friends": those in material need and those far from God, whom you help so that they become children of God and therefore friends to you.

16.5.1.en: "Mammon of unrighteousness" is the wealth of the world, considering that its distribution among people is not just, since some are born rich and some poor, and considering that many material dealings are marred by unfaithfulness and injustice; therefore money in general is called the mammon of unrighteousness.

16.5.2.en: "Ye fail": you die and leave this life.

16.5.3.en: "They may receive you": they will have died before you, and they await you in the Kingdom.

16.5.4.en: "Everlasting habitations": the lasting heavenly Kingdom, to distinguish it from the temporary, passing tents and houses of the world. Christ continues His comment, advising His children to use the world and material things by giving them to the needy, and in this way they make friends for themselves with the wealth of the world, so that these friends may bear witness for the children of God in eternity to the good works they did, and they inherit the Kingdom of Heaven.

16.6.0.en: "That which is least" is the possessions of this earthly life.

16.6.1.en: "Much" is the bliss of eternal life.

16.6.2.en: Whoever is faithful in using his life on earth to do good, God entrusts him with the inheritance of the Kingdom of Heaven; but whoever uses the world for his desires and selfishness and wrongs the needy and does not help them is not entrusted with the inheritance of the Kingdom. This means that Christ confirms the importance of faithfulness and does not commend the treachery of the unjust steward, and calls us only to imitate his wisdom, so that we are faithful during our life on earth because we are stewards from God over our bodies and all our abilities, and afterward He gives us the Kingdom as a reward.

16.7.0.en: If the "unrighteous mammon" means the wealth of this world, then the "true riches" is the inheritance of the Kingdom of Heaven. That is, faithfulness is required in the earthly life so that God may give us the Kingdom of Heaven.

16.8.0.en: We are stewards over everything we have in our earthly life because it belongs to God, and our life is not for this world, but we are created for good works which God has before ordained for us (Eph 2:10). Material things are not ours; what is ours is the virtue and righteousness that we enjoy in eternity.

16.9.0.en: Christ declared a clear truth, which is the necessity of loving God with all the heart, and using the wealth of the world as a gift from God for doing good. But if a person is attached to money, he must leave God out of his heart and become a slave of money.

16.9.1.en: Examine yourself every day: was your aim in all your thoughts, words and deeds the love of God, or the love of the world and acquiring material things???

16.10.0.en: Christ directed His words to His disciples, but there were Pharisees listening to Him. The Pharisees were marked by the love of money, so the parable and Christ's comment on it showed their sin. Instead of repenting, they scoffed at His words, fulfilling Christ's saying that whoever serves money and is attached to it rejects the word of God, since the love of money leads to pride, so that a person supposes he is superior to others by the abundance of his money, although in God's sight he is a sinner, unfaithful in distributing his money to the needy.

16.11.0.en: Christ boldly rebuked the Pharisees, because they were concerned with exalting themselves before the Jews, saying that this changes nothing because God knows the truth of your hearts, wicked and unclean with the love of pride and the love of money; for they refused to acknowledge their sin, which was the love of money, but justified themselves and neglected the work of mercy, and even supposed themselves better than those around them and the most deserving of people for the Kingdom.

16.11.1.en: Remember that you are a steward over all that you have, so use it to do good, and offer repentance in humility for every shortcoming, and God will guide you how to use your life to help the needy.

16.12.s.en: (4) The importance of the commandment, and divorce

16.12.0.en: "The law and the prophets were until John": all the teachings of the Old Testament from Moses until John the Baptist.

16.12.1.en: "Since that time": that is, after John the Baptist, and it means the proclamation of Christ.

16.12.2.en: The passing away of heaven and earth is an impossible matter because they are fixed throughout the days. This means that the Law and all the teachings of Christ are fixed throughout life, so we must submit to them and not scoff at them as the Pharisees did. "One tittle": the smallest teaching in the Old Testament.

16.12.3.en: Christ declares that His proclamation is the completion and extension of the books of the Old Testament and its prophecies, and the necessity of adhering to all the commandments; even if they are difficult in appearance, a person should hold to them and force himself to keep them, and not walk by his own desires, striving to reach the eternal Kingdom, which is better than every earthly desire.

16.13.0.en: This verse is mentioned in (Mt 5:31-32; 19:3-9). Since Christ showed the importance of God's commandments, He confronted the evil of the Pharisees who pretended to hold to them but permitted divorce for trivial reasons, such as the wife's not serving a suitable meal so that her husband divorces her. As an example of the permanence of God's commandments He declared the commandment of marriage, which preserves the structure of the family. Whoever divorces his wife and marries another commits adultery, because the first marriage still stands, and the husband left it for his own purposes, making light of the holy sacrament which the Holy Spirit accomplished. So his second marriage is invalid even if it has civil legitimacy; rather it is adultery in the sight of God and the Church. And if a man marries a divorced woman he commits adultery, because she is still in God's sight bound to her first husband, unless the divorce was for the cause that Christ declared, namely the adultery of the other party, in which case the innocent party has the right to marry. Do not distort God's word and be careless of His commandments for your own purposes, using your philosophy, but humble yourself and force yourself to keep the commandment even if it seems heavy, and God will uphold you and comfort your heart and give you in the end eternal life.

16.14.s.en: (5) The parable of the rich man and Lazarus

16.14.0.en: "Sumptuously every day": continuing in material desires and being immersed in them.

16.14.1.en: Christ gave a parable about the work of mercy and enduring suffering as a way of preparing for the Kingdom, saying: there was a rich man who was concerned with his clothing and his pleasures and desires, which He expressed by the garments of kings, that is, purple and fine linen, and he was immersed in everything the soul desires of food, drink, comfort and possessions in his great palace, with singing and dancing, and all you can imagine of the luxury of this world. He did not commit evident sins against God's commandments, but his sin was being absorbed in material things and the pleasures of the world.

16.15.0.en: "Was laid": that is, some of his acquaintances placed him before the rich man's palace, perhaps that he would have pity on him with food and treatment; this means that he was unable to move and needed someone to carry him.

16.15.1.en: "Sores": as a result of his inability to move, and his being among filth, he was exposed to microbes, so his skin peeled and blood flowed from it.

16.15.2.en: "Desiring to be fed": wishing to eat something of the rich man's scraps, but even this trivial thing that they might throw out with the garbage was not available to him; yet one of the servants in the palace may have carried some crumbs to him without the rich man's knowledge, or when the scraps were thrown outside the palace some of them were beside him and he ate a little of them.

16.15.3.en: "The dogs came": the dogs came to eat from the scraps, and found the blood flowing from his almost naked body, so they hurried to lick the sores because they love blood, and so they moistened the sores and eased his pains a little; they had more pity on him than the rich man.

16.15.4.en: At the gate of the palace of this great rich man lived a poor, naked man stricken with diseases. The rich man was occupied with his pleasures and did not feed this poor man or treat his diseases, and the poor man did not find his necessary food; he longed for the scraps thrown from the rich man's palace and found only a little of them, and for his sores he found no physician or anyone who cared for him. So it was the dogs that licked his sores and moistened them, and the poor man bore being food for the dogs that licked his blood, as he also bore all his poverty with thanksgiving and patience.

16.15.5.en: The poor man's name was "Lazarus," that is, "God is my help," so God's help upheld him so that he bore it, and he deserved to be called by name; but the rich man, because of the meanness of his life far from God, was not given a name in the parable. From the parable we sense the enormous difference between the conditions of the rich man and Lazarus in the following:-

16.15.6.en: 1- The rich man wears the finest clothes, and Lazarus is naked with his sores uncovered.

16.15.7.en: 2- The rich man is immersed in the desires of food and drink, and Lazarus longs for a little of the scraps of the rich man's food.

16.15.8.en: 3- Many serve the rich man, and Lazarus finds no one who cares for him except the dogs that came to lick his blood, not out of love for him but because he became food for them.

16.15.9.en: The rich man signifies those occupied with the desires of the world rather than the work of mercy and the love of God; for if he had loved prayer and been bound to God he would have loved the needy and helped them.

16.15.10.en: He also signifies the Jewish people, who received the knowledge of God in the commandments and the Law, but neglected to convey it to the Gentiles, and even despised them and was vexed by their evident sins, like sores, and left them in their poverty.

16.15.11.en: As for Lazarus, he signifies those who bear the afflictions of life with thanksgiving, and the Gentiles who lived in poverty and the diseases of sin for many years, but declared and confessed their sins, since sores bring blood out from inside the body to the outside, that is, confessing the inner sin openly, and so they received God's mercies in the blood of Christ the Redeemer. May you feel the needs of those around you, not only for food and material treatment but rather those far from God who suffer from sin, because they need you to show them your love and make them know a little about God, so that they are satisfied by Him and are at ease in His hands. Do not be selfishly absorbed in your wrong preoccupations, for you are responsible for offering love to all around you, and you are a steward over God's gifts and the abilities given to you, to distribute them to the needy.

16.16.0.en: "The beggar died": no concern for burying his body is mentioned; rather he died where he was without anyone's concern, but heaven hastened to welcome him.

16.16.1.en: Abraham's bosom represents all the saints rejoicing in heaven, and he is a great father to the people of God and to everyone in the world who believes. Abraham's being in Paradise before the redemption was accomplished on the cross does not trouble us, because it is a parable and not an actual story, and it expresses what will happen after the redemption is accomplished.

16.16.2.en: "The rich man also died, and was buried": people were concerned with the funeral and burial of the rich man, but his spirit found no place except in torment. The rich man's soul died because of his distance from God and his preoccupation with bodily desires, so the death of his body and his burial were a natural extension of the former death of his soul. As for Lazarus, who bore all the sufferings patiently, when he had fulfilled his labors he was taken to heaven full of many virtues, and was heavy from the abundance of virtues he carried, so he needed many angels to carry him to Paradise, to enjoy being with God and the saints. So Lazarus, who signifies the Gentiles, was in Abraham's bosom, because he believed in Christ and accepted his sufferings with thanksgiving; but the rich man, who signifies the Jews, because of his selfishness went far from his father Abraham, the father of faith, and was cast into hell and eternal torment.

16.17.0.en: "He lifted up his eyes": confirms that hell is in a lower place and Paradise in a lofty place; this is in the moral sense and not the material, that is, Paradise is an exalted state and hell a low state. "Afar off": declares this distance between Paradise, the place where the righteous wait, and hell, the place where the wicked wait. As a result of this rich man's selfishness and his immersion in material desires, he was cast into hell, the place where the wicked wait after this life, and there he faced severe torment, expressed by the flame and the severe pain in his tongue and by its being a lower place; and he lifted up his eyes to Paradise, the place where the righteous wait, and found Lazarus enjoying himself in Abraham's bosom, with whom all the Jews hope to be in Paradise, and he asked for even a drop of water from Lazarus's finger to cool his tongue. This rich man who was stingy toward Lazarus with the crumbs that fell from his table became a beggar and did not receive.

16.17.1.en: A person's tongue is what leads him to eternal happiness or eternal torment, and because of the rich man's great arrogance and his much talk about material desires, his tongue suffered severe pain as he called out to Abraham, "Father Abraham," but he had lost his sonship by his evil and was in torment.

16.18.0.en: Abraham's reply to the rich man was that the torment he suffers is his natural recompense, because he was immersed in material desires and made himself independent of the knowledge of God by them, while Lazarus bore the calamities with thanksgiving from God's hand, and so deserved comfort and eternal joy.

16.18.1.en: If you bear sufferings with thanksgiving, or lose some material things, do not be disturbed, because God compensates you for them in heaven.

16.19.0.en: Abraham gave another reason for not granting his request, which is that there is a gulf between hell and Paradise that prevents anyone from passing from one to the other. This means that the condition in heaven is fixed, either in torment or in bliss, and there is no mixing between the righteous and the wicked, but they see one another, so the righteous are comforted and thank God when they see the torment of the wicked, and the torment of the wicked increases if they look at the happiness of the righteous, from which they are deprived forever.

16.20.0.en: After the rich man despaired of having his pains eased, he made another request of Abraham, which was to send Lazarus to the earth to warn the rich man's five brothers so that they would repent, because they walk like their brother and are absorbed in material pleasures, that they might not come to the place of torment. By his request the rich man wanted his torment not to increase by seeing his brothers with him in hell, especially since he may have been a cause of their absorption in desires, because he was an example to them.

16.20.1.en: The five brothers signify the five senses, which, if they are not sanctified in Christ, are immersed in desires and lead a person to eternal torment.

16.21.0.en: From the preceding dialogue it appears that those who have departed, even the wicked among them who are in hell, see those on earth and wish their salvation by repentance and life with God, but Abraham's reply to the rich man was that they have the books of the Old Testament, and this shows the importance of the Old Testament for a person's salvation and repentance. This parable also answers the heresy of the transmigration of souls, which proclaims that the spirit is incarnated in several bodies until it is purified of its sins and rises to the higher spirit. For instead of the rich man's being tormented, he could have been incarnated in a lowly body, as this heresy says.

16.22.0.en: The rich man said to Abraham that the rising of one from the dead would alert those careless about the salvation of their souls to repent, but Abraham objected, declaring that whoever does not repent by reading the Holy Bible will not benefit from the rising of one from the dead, because the word of God, that is, Christ who is in the Scripture, is stronger than all for whoever wants to hear. Lazarus the brother of Mary and Martha rose from the dead when Christ raised him, and the Jews did not repent but tried to kill him; and likewise Christ rose from the dead and they did not repent either, but persecuted His disciples.

16.22.1.en: Take care to read the Holy Bible every day and obey it as a personal message to you from God.

16.22.2.en: How we prepare for the end of the days. Offences (vv. 1-2):

16.22.3.en: 1- Then said he unto the disciples, "It is impossible but that offences will come: but woe unto him, through whom they come! 2- It were better for him that a millstone were hanged about his neck, and he cast into the sea, than that he should offend one of these little ones.
